blocos.texto: (or: the case of place — and the little secret of open and closed places)

blocos.explicacao: A scene you have lived (or will). You already know how to conjugate verbs, use the past, the future and the accusative case. Now imagine another scene. You are in Russia. You want to say you are in your room. You think: "room in Russian is ко́мната. I'll say я в ко́мната." The person gives you a strange look and corrects you: — Я в ко́мнате. You look again. It is the same word, ко́мната. But now it ends in -е, not -а. You think: "Why? I already changed this word for the accusative (ко́мнату). Has it changed again? How many forms does this word have?" This happens to every Russian learner, and it happens because you have just met the prepositional case. It sounds like one more complicated case. It is not. Five minutes of careful reading and you will understand the little secret that solves everything. What is the prepositional case, and why is it called that? First, a question: why is this case called prepositional? Memorise this: the prepositional case is the only case in Russian that NEVER appears alone. It always comes after a preposition. That is where the name comes from: it is the case "of the preposition". It does not exist without one. Never, in any sentence, in any context. The nominative can appear alone (это дом), the accusative can appear alone (я вижу дом), but the prepositional always has a preposition before it. Always. And what is it for? Here is the answer: the prepositional case is used to say WHERE things are. It is the case of place. When you want to say "I am in the room", "I live in Russia", "the book is on the table", "I work at the factory", in all of these sentences the noun goes into the prepositional case. It is the "where" case. As simple as that. (It is also used with the preposition «о» to say what you are talking or thinking "about".) English puts all the meaning in the little words "in", "on", "at", and the noun never changes. Russian changes both the little word and the ending of the noun.

blocos.titulo: The little secret: open places and closed places
blocos.explicacao: The little secret: open places and closed places. Now comes the most charming part. Pay attention, because here is the key to everything. Russian has two main prepositions for "where": В and НА. Both can mean "in", "on" or "at". But Russian chooses between them with a very simple logic. В → for CLOSED places: places you can go inside, places with walls, doors, an interior. НА → for OPEN, WIDE places: places where you are on, on top of, on the surface. The magic test: ask yourself, can you go inside? YES → В (shop, room, cinema, theatre, house, school, factory, restaurant, museum...). NO, it is a wide, open place → НА (square, street, park, station, market, mountain, river...). Look at how it works. Комната (room): you can go inside → В. Магазин (shop): you can go inside → В. Площадь (square): wide, open → НА. Улица (street): open → НА. Работа (work): not a physical place but an activity → НА. Урок (lesson): not a place but an event → НА. Концерт (concert): not a place but an event → НА. The general rule: can you go inside? If yes, В. If it is wide, open, or an event or activity, НА. English does something similar, only less neatly: you are "in" the room but "on" the street, "at" the station, "at" a concert, "at" work. (A few words, like почта, break the logic. Learn them as exceptions.)

blocos.titulo: The bridge with English: В = in, НА = on / at
blocos.explicacao: The bridge with English: В = in, НА = on / at. Here is the nicest thing: you already do this in English without noticing. You say: I am in the room. I am in the shop. I am in the cinema. I am on the square. I am on the street. I am at the station. English picks "in", "on" or "at" depending on the place, and sometimes it is hard to explain why (on the bus, in the car, at work). Russian does the same with just two words. The preposition В works like our "in". The preposition НА works like our "on / at", with a nuance of "on top of, on the surface". Compare. Notice that the preposition is a separate word, never merged into the noun. But the idea is the same as in English. You only have to choose between В (closed) and НА (open / event). And do not forget the second half: the noun changes its ending (комната → комнате).

blocos.titulo: The 4 main prepositions of the prepositional case
blocos.explicacao: The 4 main prepositions of the prepositional case. The prepositional case is governed by four main prepositions. Let's meet each one. • 1. В (in, inside). Use: closed places you can go inside. Question: Где? (Where?) Examples follow. Spelling variant: ВО. Before words that begin with в or ф followed by another consonant, ВО is used instead of В. Why? Euphony. Russian does not like certain consonant clusters: «в Владивостоке» would sound bad, so an -о- is inserted to separate them. • 2. НА (on, at). Use: open, wide places, or events and activities. Question: Где? (Where?) Examples follow. Notice that на also appears with places that "make no sense" (почта, работа, урок, концерт). The logic is not only "open vs. closed": it also includes events, activities and surfaces. And there are historical exceptions, which we will see later. • 3. О (about, concerning). Use: to talk about something. Question: О ком? О чём? (About whom? About what?) Examples follow. Spelling variants: ОБ and ОБО. О goes before a consonant: о кни́ге, о рабо́те, о теа́тре. ОБ goes before a vowel: об Ива́не, об А́нне, об э́том, об о́сени. ОБО goes before мне, всём, всех and a few other words that start with a hard consonant cluster: обо мне, обо всём, обо льде. Why? Euphony again. «О Иване» would sound bad, and «о мне» too. So Russian inserts об or обо to keep the vowels and consonants apart. (You do this in English with "a" / "an": a book, an apple.) • 4. ПРИ (at, in the presence of, in the time of). Use: rare in daily life, but it appears in formal and historical contexts and in contexts of closeness. ПРИ has three meanings: • 1. Attached to, next to: при университе́те (attached to the university). • 2. In the presence of: при де́тях (in front of the children). • 3. In the time of: при царе́ (in the time of the tsar).

blocos.titulo: в and на: choosing by the picture of the place
blocos.explicacao: Both mean «in / at / on», but Russian chooses by picture. «В» = inside a closed or bounded space: в доме, в комнате, в сумке, and also countries and cities (в России, в Москве). «На» = on a surface (на столе, на полу, на стене), in a place seen as open space (на улице, на площади, на море) or at an event or activity (на работе, на уроке, на концерте). The word after в/на goes into the prepositional case (-е, -и): в доме, на столе. Some short masculine nouns have a prepositional in -у when they answer «где?»: в шкафу, в саду, в лесу, на полу, на мосту.
blocos.comparacao: English also uses «in / on / at», but not in the same places: Russian says «на работе» (literally «on work») and «на уроке» (literally «on the lesson»). The choice between в and на depends on the picture of the place: inside, on top, open space or event.
